4º de Primaria · Inglés · Tema 7

Food and shopping: some and any

Nombre: ______________________   Fecha: ___________

Qué vas a aprender

  • Learn food words and containers (a bottle of, a packet of)
  • Use some in affirmative sentences and any in negatives and questions
  • Ask for things in a shop politely
  • Ask and answer about prices with How much is it?
  • Tell countable and uncountable nouns apart
  • Ask How many…? and How much…?
  • Order food politely in a café
  • Talk about food groups and follow a simple recipe

Para pensar

Vas a una tienda en Inglaterra. Quieres comprar manzanas, pero no sabes cuántas hay. ¿Cómo preguntarías «¿Hay manzanas?»?

Explicación

1. Food words

Let's review some food: apples, bananas, oranges, tomatoes, carrots, potatoes, eggs, bread (pan), cheese (queso), milk (leche), water, juice (zumo), rice (arroz), pasta, chicken (pollo), fish and meat (carne).

Some food words have a plural with -s: one apple, two apples; one tomato, three tomatoes. Others don't, like bread, milk, rice or water: we can't count them one by one. En castellano: pasa igual en español: no decimos «tres arroces».

2. A, an or some?

For one thing we can count, we use a or an: a banana, a carrot, an apple, an egg (we use an before a vowel sound: a, e, i, o, u).

For more than one thing, or for things we can't count, we use some: some bananas, some eggs, some bread, some milk. En castellano: some es «unos», «unas» o «un poco de». «I've got some cheese» = «Tengo (un poco de) queso». Muchas veces en español ni lo traducimos.

3. Countable and uncountable

In English, nouns can be countable (contables) or uncountable (incontables):

  • Countable nouns are things we can count: one apple, two apples, three eggs, four bananas. They have a singular and a plural form. We use a / an in the singular: an apple, a banana.
  • Uncountable nouns are things we can't count one by one: water, milk, bread, rice, cheese, sugar, juice, money, homework. They have no plural and we never use a / an with them. We say «some water», not «a water» or «waters».

To count uncountable things, we use containers or quantities:

  • a glass of water, a bottle of milk
  • a slice of bread (una rebanada), a piece of cheese
  • a bowl of rice, a cup of tea
  • a kilo of sugar

Be careful! Some words are countable in Spanish but uncountable in English: bread (pan), fruit (fruta), information, homework (deberes), hair (pelo). We say «I've got long hair» and «I've got some homework», never «hairs» or «homeworks».

4. Some in affirmative sentences

We use some in affirmative sentences (frases afirmativas): «There are some oranges in the fridge», «I've got some sandwiches for the trip», «We need some water».

We also use some when we offer or ask for something politely: «Would you like some cake?» (¿quieres un poco de pastel?), «Can I have some juice, please?». Consejo: en estas preguntas usamos some porque esperamos que la respuesta sea «sí».

5. Any in negatives and questions

We use any in negative sentences and in questions: «There aren't any bananas» (no hay plátanos), «I haven't got any money» (no tengo dinero), «Is there any milk?», «Are there any eggs?».

Remember the short answers: «Yes, there is. / No, there isn't.», «Yes, there are. / No, there aren't.». En castellano: en las negativas any equivale a «nada de» o «ningún»: «There isn't any bread» = «No hay (nada de) pan».

6. How many? How much?

To ask about quantity, we use two different questions:

  • How many + countable nouns in plural: «How many apples are there?» → «There are five apples.» «How many eggs do you need?» → «Three.»
  • How much + uncountable nouns: «How much milk is there?» → «There's a litre.» «How much sugar do you want?» → «Just a little.»

Possible answers:

  • With countable: a lot, a few (unos pocos), not many, none. «There are a lot of oranges, but there are only a few lemons.»
  • With uncountable: a lot, a little (un poco), not much, none. «There's a lot of water, but there's only a little juice.»

Remember that How much is it? also means ¿Cuánto cuesta? because money is uncountable. «How much is the sandwich?» → «It's three euros.» «How much are the apples?» → «They're two euros a kilo.»

A trick: if you can put a number in front of the noun (three eggs), use how many. If you can't (three milks? No!), use how much.

7. Containers and quantities

To buy food we often use containers (envases): a bottle of water (una botella de agua), a carton of milk (un brik de leche), a packet of biscuits (un paquete de galletas), a tin of tuna (una lata de atún), a jar of jam (un tarro de mermelada), a bag of potatoes (una bolsa de patatas), a loaf of bread (una barra de pan).

We also use weights: a kilo of apples, half a kilo of cheese. Don't forget the word of in the middle!

8. At the shop: asking politely

In a shop, the shop assistant (dependiente) says: «Can I help you?» or «What would you like?». You answer: «Can I have a kilo of tomatoes, please?» or «I'd like some bread, please».

At the end you say «That's all, thank you» (eso es todo). En castellano: en inglés es muy importante decir please y thank you. Pedir algo sin «please» suena maleducado, aunque en español a veces digamos solo «Ponme un kilo de tomates».

9. At the café: ordering food

When you go to a café or a restaurant in an English-speaking country, these phrases are very useful:

The waiter / waitress says:

  • «Are you ready to order?» (¿Están listos para pedir?)
  • «What would you like?» / «What can I get you?»
  • «Anything else?» (¿Algo más?)
  • «Would you like a dessert?»
  • «Here you are.» (Aquí tiene.)

The customer says:

  • «Can I have a cheese sandwich, please?»
  • «I'd like some orange juice, please.» (I'd like = I would like: me gustaría. It's very polite.)
  • «Is there any meat in this?»
  • «No, thank you. That's all.»
  • «Can I have the bill, please?» (la cuenta)

Typical British food you can find in a café:

  • sandwiches: cheese, ham, tuna, egg
  • jacket potato: a big baked potato with beans or cheese
  • scones: little cakes with jam and cream
  • fish and chips
  • a cup of tea with milk

Never say «Give me…». It sounds rude in English. Always use Can I have…? or I'd like… and don't forget please and thank you!

10. How much is it?

To ask the price, we say: «How much is it?» (¿cuánto es?) for one thing, and «How much are they?» for more than one. The answer: «It's two euros», «They're one euro fifty».

Prices in English: €3.50 is «three euros fifty»; £1.20 is «one pound twenty». En castellano: en inglés los decimales se escriben con punto, no con coma: 2.50, no 2,50. Y el símbolo de la moneda va delante: €5, £5, $5.

11. Reading: the picnic

Read: «Tomorrow Irene and her friends are going to have a picnic. Irene looks in the kitchen. There's some bread and there are some tomatoes. There's some cheese, but there isn't any ham. There aren't any crisps and there isn't any juice! She writes a shopping list: a packet of ham, two bags of crisps, a bottle of orange juice. At the shop she asks: "How much is it?" "It's six euros forty." "Here you are. Thank you!"»

What is there in the kitchen? What does Irene buy?

12. Let's practise: the class shop

Turn the classroom into a shop. Some students are shop assistants and others are customers. Make price labels and use toy food or pictures. Each customer has a shopping list and €10 in paper money.

Customer: «Good morning! Have you got any eggs?» Assistant: «Yes, we have. / Sorry, we haven't got any.» Customer: «Can I have some eggs, please? How much are they?». Consejo: recuerda: some para afirmar y pedir; any para preguntar si hay y para decir que no hay.

13. A healthy plate

To be healthy, we need to eat different types of food every day. Food is divided into food groups:

  • Fruit and vegetables: apples, oranges, carrots, lettuce, tomatoes… They give us vitamins. They should be about half of our plate!
  • Cereals (cereales): bread, rice, pasta, potatoes. They give us energy.
  • Proteins (proteínas): meat, fish, eggs, beans, lentils. They help us to grow and make our muscles strong.
  • Dairy (lácteos): milk, cheese, yoghurt. They make our bones and teeth strong.
  • Fats (grasas): olive oil, nuts. We need a little, every day.

Some food is OK only sometimes: sweets, crisps, cakes, fizzy drinks. They have a lot of sugar, salt or fat.

And remember to drink water!

Let's describe a healthy lunch: «On my plate, there's some rice, some chicken and a lot of salad. There aren't any chips. For dessert, I have an orange. I drink a glass of water.»

Experts also say that it's a good idea to eat five portions of fruit and vegetables every day, and to eat food of many different colours: red tomatoes, green broccoli, orange carrots, purple grapes. A colourful plate is a healthy plate!

What's on your plate today? Is it a healthy plate?

14. A recipe: fruit salad

A recipe (receta) tells us how to cook something. It has two parts: the ingredients and the method (the steps). In the method, we use the imperative: the verb at the beginning, without a subject: Wash, Cut, Mix.

Fruit salad (for four people)

Ingredients:

  • two apples
  • two bananas
  • an orange
  • a bunch of grapes (un racimo de uvas)
  • some strawberries
  • some orange juice
  • a little honey (optional)

Method:

  1. Wash all the fruit carefully.
  2. Peel (pela) the bananas and the orange.
  3. Cut the fruit into small pieces. Ask an adult to help you with the knife!
  4. Put all the fruit in a big bowl.
  5. Add the orange juice and a little honey.
  6. Mix everything with a spoon.
  7. Put the bowl in the fridge for thirty minutes.
  8. Serve and enjoy!

Did you know? Fruit salad is a perfect dessert, because it has vitamins and no added sugar, and you can use the fruit of each season.

Notice the words first, then, next and finally: we can use them to put the steps in order.

Some and any

Ejercicios

  1. Translate: pan, queso, leche, huevos.

  2. Complete with a or an: ___ orange, ___ banana.

  3. Complete: «There are ___ apples in the bag.» (some/any)

  4. Complete: «Is there ___ juice?» (some/any)

  5. Complete: «We haven't got ___ rice.» (some/any)

  6. Translate: un paquete de galletas, una lata de atún.

  7. How do you ask the price of one thing?

  8. Say the price: €1.20.

  9. Short answer (no): «Are there any bananas?»

  10. Write your shopping list for a picnic (4 items).

  11. Countable or uncountable: milk?

  12. Complete: How ___ eggs are there?

  13. What does «I'd like» mean?

  14. Name two dairy products.

  15. Complete: a ___ of water.

  16. Complete: How ___ sugar do you want?

  17. Correct: I have a lot of homeworks.

  18. Write how to ask for the bill.

  19. Write the first three steps of the fruit salad.

  20. Answer: How much is the sandwich? (3 €)

  21. Write a café dialogue with four turns.

  22. Describe a healthy lunch with some, any and a lot of.

  23. Write a recipe for a sandwich with imperatives.

  24. Make a menu for a class café with prices.

Practica

  1. «There are ___ tomatoes.»

    1. A) any
    2. B) a
    3. C) some

  2. «There isn't ___ water.»

    1. A) any
    2. B) some
    3. C) a

  3. «Are there ___ oranges?»

    1. A) some
    2. B) any
    3. C) an

  4. «___ egg»

    1. A) a
    2. B) an
    3. C) some

  5. «Can I have ___ juice, please?»

    1. A) any
    2. B) a
    3. C) some

  6. «Una botella de agua» is…

    1. A) a bottle of water
    2. B) a water bottle of
    3. C) a bottle water

  7. «¿Cuánto es?» is…

    1. A) How many is it?
    2. B) What price it is?
    3. C) How much is it?

  8. Which food can't we count?

    1. A) carrot
    2. B) rice
    3. C) egg

  9. €2.50 is…

    1. A) two euros fifty
    2. B) two fifty euros
    3. C) two euros and half

  10. What does a shop assistant say?

    1. A) Can I help you?
    2. B) Can you help me?
    3. C) How much are you?

  11. Which is uncountable?

    1. A) apple
    2. B) rice
    3. C) egg

  12. How ___ apples do you want?

    1. A) much
    2. B) any
    3. C) many

  13. The polite way to order is…

    1. A) Give me…
    2. B) I'd like…
    3. C) I want it.

  14. Fruit and vegetables give us…

    1. A) vitamins
    2. B) only fat
    3. C) sugar

  15. In a recipe, «Cut the fruit» is…

    1. A) a question
    2. B) a negative
    3. C) an imperative

Explícalo con tus palabras

Incluye: Qué comida se puede contar y cuál no; Cuándo se usa a, an y some; Cuándo se usa any; Cómo se pide algo y se pregunta el precio en una tienda.
